title: The Holy Spirit: A Bible Study on the Forgotten God
subtitle: A five-session study on the Holy Spirit, the personal presence of God who gives life.
summary:
This study is for small groups, adult classes and individuals who have spent years in church and somehow ended up with two persons of the Trinity they could describe and a third they couldn't. The Father they can picture. The Son they love. The Spirit has been left a kind of holy vapor, a power source, the part of God you mention at the end of a prayer and then forget. That isn't a small mistake. It's losing sight of God himself, present, personal and living in his people, the breath by which the dead are made alive.

The five sessions take up who the Spirit is and why we treat him as an afterthought; the new birth, in which the Spirit raises the spiritually dead and does what argument never could; the slow growth of his fruit, and the difference between being changed and performing; the contested question of the gifts, where continuationists and cessationists are both given their strongest case and the group is held together across the divide; and the Spirit in our weakness, who prays in us when we have no words and is the down payment of a world being made new.

This study won't pick the group's side in the old arguments over tongues, prophecy and healing, and no leader should let it. Each case is set out at full strength, and the aim is a room that can disagree about the gifts while worshiping the same Spirit. None of us stands outside what this study names. I don't, and neither will you.
audience: Small groups, adult Sunday school, and individuals

sessions.title: The Spirit We Ignore
sessions.aim: To recover the Holy Spirit as fully God and fully personal, not a force the church switches on for emotional moments and forgets the rest of the time, and to face plainly why we've made the third person of the Trinity an afterthought.
sessions.summary:
Ask most Christians who the Holy Spirit is and you'll get a long pause, then something about a feeling, a power, an influence. They can describe the Father and the Son. The Spirit they can't, and that loss isn't academic. Francis Chan called his book on this Forgotten God, and the title fits.

There are two opposite errors, and each holds something true. One treats the Spirit as a force, a kind of divine electricity that fills you and makes you feel things. It's right that the Spirit is power and does fill. The other is so wary of emotionalism that it files the Spirit away in the doctrine of God, true on paper and absent from life. It's right to fear a faith that hunts for feelings.

Scripture won't let either win. The Spirit can be grieved, lied to and resisted, and only a person can be grieved. And he isn't a footnote, because he's God himself living in his people. He's God, of one being with the Father and the Son. He's personal: he speaks, wills and loves. And he's here. We forget him not because he's unimportant but because he's humble. He points to Christ, and we mistook his quietness for absence.

keyScripture.why: "And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth ... he dwells with you and will be in you" (John 14:16-17). The Spirit isn't a force sent from far off but a personal presence, God himself, who comes to live in his people.

discussion.q: Before tonight, if someone had asked who the Holy Spirit is, what would you have said? How does that compare with how you'd describe the Father and the Son?
discussion.behind: Bring the gap into the open before you correct anything. Most people can describe the Father and the Son and go vague on the Spirit, and saying so out loud is the point of the opening. Don't rush to fix it. Let the room feel how much has been missing, and go first if it's slow.

discussion.q: We often talk about the Spirit as a power we switch on: "the Spirit fell," "I felt the Spirit." Where have you caught yourself thinking of the Spirit as something God uses rather than as God himself?
discussion.behind: Notice the grammar of our forgetting. We say things about the Spirit we'd never say about the Father. Do it gently, so people see they've been treating God as a vapor without meaning to.

discussion.q: Read Ephesians 4:30 and Acts 5:3-4. Scripture says the Spirit can be grieved and lied to. What changes when you realize you can hurt the Spirit the way you hurt someone who loves you?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. The Spirit's personhood isn't a doctrine for its own sake; it's a relationship. Grieving the Spirit isn't tripping a circuit but hurting Someone, which is more sobering and more tender than the force picture allows.

discussion.q: Read John 16:13-14. Jesus says the Spirit "will not speak on his own authority" and "will glorify me." How does that change the way you read the Spirit's apparent quietness?
discussion.behind: The Spirit's self-effacement isn't absence. It's his character. Help the room stop reading his lack of self-promotion as a reason to ignore him and start reading it as what it is: a person who delights to honor another.

discussion.q: Many of us confess the Trinity on Sunday and then pray and live as if the Spirit weren't in the room. Where have you held the doctrine on paper while living as though God were far away?
discussion.behind: You're not hunting for confessions. You want each person, starting with you, to admit the gap between the creed we say and the absence we live. Go first. The candor here opens the rest of the study.

objections.objection: The Spirit is the power of God, plainly, the energy that fills believers and makes things happen. Calling him a person reads too much into poetic language about wind and fire and breath.
objections.response: Half of this is true. The Spirit is power, Scripture says so, and the pictures of wind and fire and living water tell us he fills and moves and gives life. But the same Scripture says Ananias lied "to the Holy Spirit" (Acts 5:3), tells the Ephesians, "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God" (Ephesians 4:30), and has Stephen tell his accusers, "you always resist the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:51). You can't lie to electricity or grieve the wind. You can only lie to, grieve and resist someone. The Spirit is called the Helper. He teaches, intercedes, wills and speaks, and Jesus warned that blasphemy against him will not be forgiven (Matthew 12:31). A force does none of that. The power is real, but it belongs to a person, and to keep the power while losing the person is to keep the gift and lose the Giver.

objections.objection: All this talk of the Spirit as a presence inside you is exactly what leads to the emotionalism I've seen, people chasing feelings and calling every impulse the Spirit. Better to keep him safely in the doctrine of God.
objections.response: Much of that is right. Real harm has been done in the Spirit's name: impulses treated as guidance, manipulation passed off as anointing, a hunger for experience that left people exhausted and deceived. A healthy fear of that is wise. But walling the Spirit off in a doctrine so he never touches your actual life is its own error, because the Spirit Jesus promised wasn't a clause in a creed. He was a presence "to be with you forever" (John 14:16). The answer to bad experience isn't no experience. It's the Spirit tested by the Word, since the Spirit who inspired Scripture never contradicts it. Don't chase every feeling. But don't send the living God into exile because some have abused his name.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If the Holy Spirit is a person who can be grieved, when did you last consider that the way you've lived might have hurt Someone who loves you, rather than only broken a rule?
sessions.practice: This week, change one thing in how you pray. Instead of mentioning the Spirit only at the end, or not at all, begin once a day by speaking to the Spirit directly and simply, as someone present: "Holy Spirit, you're here. Help me." Don't try to produce anything. Just practice speaking to the God who lives in you as the person he is, and write down whether speaking to him rather than about him changed anything.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, we confess that we've known your Son and called on your name and left your Spirit a stranger, a power we used and a person we forgot. Forgive us for grieving the One we treated as a force. You are God, of one being with the Father and the Son, and you've come to live in us, and we've lived as though the house were empty. Open our eyes to the presence we've ignored. Holy Spirit, humble and quiet, always pointing to Christ, we welcome you, not as a feeling we chase but as the God who is already here. Amen.
reflection: Where have I worshiped two persons of the Trinity and left the third a vapor, and what has that cost me without my noticing?
If the Spirit can be grieved, what in my life this week has hurt Someone rather than simply broken a rule?
What would change if I lived all day as though God weren't far above me but living in me, present in the next ordinary moment?
sessions.teaching:
Here's a test most of us would fail. Ask a room of lifelong Christians to describe the Father, and they'll manage it. Ask them to describe the Son, and they'll do better, because they have a face, a life, a cross to picture. Then ask who the Holy Spirit is, and watch the pause. Something about a power. A feeling. An influence that comes over you in worship. Francis Chan called his book on this Forgotten God, and the title is a charge we've earned. We haven't only mislaid a doctrine. We've reduced a person of the Godhead to a vapor, and we did it so quietly we never noticed the room had gone empty.

So I don't want to start with what the Spirit does, which is where most of us want to start, hungry for power or gifts or guidance. I want to start with the harder question: who is he?

There are two errors that pull against each other, and each deserves a fair hearing. The first treats the Spirit as a force, an "it," a divine current that fills you and lifts you and makes you feel God near. There's a true instinct in that. The Spirit really is power, and he really does fill. The pictures Scripture gives aren't decoration: the rushing wind at Pentecost, the tongues of fire, the living water, the breath of God. Strip all that away and you lose something real. The second error runs the other way. It's so wary of emotionalism that it files the Spirit under the doctrine of God, affirmed in the creed and absent from the week. There's a true instinct there too: a proper fear of a faith that becomes a hunt for sensations and calls every impulse divine.

Scripture won't let either one take the whole field. Against the first, the Spirit isn't a force, and the evidence is simple. Paul writes, "do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God" (Ephesians 4:30). Peter asks Ananias why he has lied "to the Holy Spirit," and then says, "You have not lied to man but to God" (Acts 5:3-4). Stephen tells his accusers, "you always resist the Holy Spirit" (Acts 7:51). Think about what those verbs require. You can't grieve electricity or lie to the wind. And the Spirit speaks: "Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them" (Acts 13:2). He gives gifts "to each one individually as he wills" (1 Corinthians 12:11). Those are the acts of a person.

It's worth slowing down on that word "grieve," because we've flattened it. You don't grieve over a stranger, and a stranger isn't grieved by you. Grief belongs to someone close, someone whose face changes when you wound them. Paul is telling us that the God who lives in us is near enough and personal enough to be hurt by how we live, not the way a rule is broken but the way a friendship is bruised. Once you feel the difference between tripping a wire and wounding a friend, the force picture of the Spirit falls apart in your hands.

Against the second error, the Spirit isn't a footnote, because what Jesus promised wasn't a line in a doctrine. "I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth ... he dwells with you and will be in you" (John 14:16-17). "Another" means another like Jesus himself, a personal presence, not a downgrade to an influence. "With you" and "in you" mean God himself coming to live inside his people. "I will not leave you as orphans," Jesus said (John 14:18). So the Spirit is God, of one being with the Father and the Son. He's personal: he speaks and wills and loves and can be grieved. And he's here, nearer than your breath, and in both Hebrew and Greek the word for Spirit is also the word for breath.

Then why do we forget him? Not because he's unimportant. Because he's humble. Jesus said of him, "he will not speak on his own authority ... He will glorify me" (John 16:13-14). The Spirit's delight is to turn the light onto Christ and stay out of it himself, and we, trained to notice whatever promotes itself, took his self-effacement for absence. That's the world's logic, where the loudest voice is assumed to matter most, and we carried it straight into our reading of God.

I include myself in this. Many of us can confess the Trinity on Sunday morning, all three persons fully God, and then pray that afternoon as if we were calling up to a distant sky, and live all week as though the house were empty. The forgetting isn't someone else's problem. It's ours. And all the while the Spirit has been in the room, humble, glorifying Christ, and waiting with a patience that ought to undo us, to be known.

scriptureStudy.note: "He will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth ... he dwells with you and will be in you." "Another" means another of the same kind as Jesus, a person and not an influence, and "with" and "in" name a presence, not a distant power.
"And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption." You can't grieve a force. The command assumes a person who can be wounded by how his people live.
Peter tells Ananias he has lied "to the Holy Spirit," then says, "You have not lied to man but to God." In one breath the Spirit is named as the one lied to and as God.
"All these are empowered by one and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills." The Spirit wills, chooses and gives, which is the action of a person with a mind.
"The Holy Spirit said, 'Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.'" The Spirit speaks, calls, and claims a work as his own.
"And the Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters." From the first page the Spirit is present and active in creation, no latecomer to the story.
"Anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him." The Spirit's presence is the mark of belonging to Christ, not an optional power for a few special believers.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at the long argument the church had before it said plainly what it believes about the Spirit. In the fourth century a group arose, later called the Pneumatomachi, "fighters against the Spirit," who would grant that the Spirit was more than a creature but would not call him fully God. Athanasius wrote against such views in his letters to Serapion, and Basil of Caesarea, in his treatise On the Holy Spirit (about 375), argued that the Spirit is to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, which only makes sense if the Spirit is God. The Council of Constantinople in 381 expanded the Nicene Creed to confess the Spirit as "the Lord and giver of life," who with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified.

Ask why the church wouldn't let this go. If the Spirit who lives in you isn't fully God, then God doesn't actually dwell in you; something less than God does. The deity of the Spirit is the difference between God present and a messenger sent. Then set that beside the vague spirituality of our own time, with its talk of energy and presence and the universe, and ask what's lost when the Spirit becomes a feeling again rather than the Lord and giver of life the church labored to confess.

memoryVerse.text: And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Helper, to be with you forever, even the Spirit of truth. You know him, for he dwells with you and will be in you.

sessions.title: Born of the Spirit
sessions.aim: To take the new birth as the Spirit's work and not ours, to see regeneration as God raising the spiritually dead rather than coaching the spiritually struggling, and to see that the Spirit does what argument never could.
sessions.summary:
Jesus tells a religious teacher, a man who had done everything right, that he must be born again, born of the Spirit, or he won't even see the kingdom of God. The first question is why Jesus aims his hardest words about new birth not at the worst sinner in town but at one of the most respectable men in Israel.

The answer is that the new birth isn't improvement. It's resurrection. You didn't contribute to your first birth, and you don't author your second. Many people feel strongly that conversion is simply a decision we make, and there's something real in that: we do believe, repent and come, and we're responsible for coming. But Jesus won't let the human decision swallow God's act. The Spirit is like the wind, he says, blowing where it wishes. You hear it, but you can't command it.

Then the hopeful turn. If the new birth is the Spirit's work, no one is beyond it: not the hardest skeptic, not the most cynical heart. The same Spirit who hovered over the waters and raised Christ from the tomb makes the dead alive, and the dead don't improve their way to life. They're raised.

keyScripture.why: "Unless one is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God ... The wind blows where it wishes" (John 3:5, 8). Jesus names the new birth as God's sovereign work, not the achievement of the one being born.

discussion.q: Read John 3:1-8. Jesus tells one of the most respectable, religious men in Israel that he must be born again. Why do you think those words land on the good man and not on an obvious sinner?
discussion.behind: We expect the call to be born again to go to the prostitute and the tax collector. Jesus aims it at a Pharisee. Bring out the assumption that respectability gives us a head start with God, and let the room feel that the new birth levels everyone, the moral and the immoral alike.

discussion.q: If the new birth is like a birth, you contribute to it about as much as you contributed to your first one. How does that sit with you?
discussion.behind: Most of us are deeply attached to the idea that we did something to be saved. Let people feel both the offense and the relief of Jesus's picture: a baby doesn't assist in being born. Let that reframe what conversion is.

discussion.q: Many Christians would say conversion is simply a decision we make. What's true in that? What does it leave out about the Spirit as the wind that "blows where it wishes"?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves carefully. We really do decide, believe and repent, and you mustn't deny human responsibility. What's missing is treating the decision as the whole cause. Help the room hold the mystery, that we truly choose and the Spirit truly raises, without flattening either side.

discussion.q: If coming to faith were only a matter of being persuaded, what would be missing?
discussion.behind: Help the room feel the limits of argument. Many assume people outside the faith just need the right case made. Arguments matter, but information doesn't raise the dead. Seeing that changes how we pray for the people we love.

discussion.q: If the new birth is the Spirit's work and not the sinner's achievement, how should that change the way you pray for the hardest, most cynical person you know?
discussion.behind: We give up on people we think are too far gone, which quietly assumes their salvation depends on their openness rather than the Spirit's power. Invite people to name that person to themselves and to pray differently. Go first.

objections.objection: Conversion is a decision a person makes. You weigh the evidence, you choose to believe, and the choosing is yours. Talk of the Spirit raising the dead takes away human freedom and makes us puppets.
objections.response: There's something real here. We do decide. The gospel says believe, repent and come, and means it. The one who comes is responsible for coming, and the one who refuses is responsible for refusing. None of that is denied. But notice what a decision can't account for. Jesus doesn't tell Nicodemus to decide harder. He tells him he must be born again, born of the Spirit, and a birth isn't something you perform on yourself. Paul says that "even when we were dead in our trespasses," God "made us alive together with Christ" (Ephesians 2:5). The church has long held that the same event is fully the Spirit's work and truly your response, the wind that blows where it wishes and the sail that really catches it. To shrink it to your decision alone is to make yourself the author of your own resurrection.

objections.objection: If the new birth is entirely the Spirit's work and the wind blows where it wishes, why evangelize at all? And why is it the sinner's fault if he isn't born again?
objections.response: This is one of the oldest hard questions, and you shouldn't pretend it away. On evangelism: the Spirit ordinarily works through the word being spoken. "Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ" (Romans 10:17). So the Spirit's freedom isn't a reason for silence. It's the only reason our words have any power, since we can't raise the dead and he can. On fault: Scripture never lets the sinner off the hook. No one is turned away who wanted to come, every refusal is a real and willing refusal, and everyone who comes is welcomed. The Bible holds the Spirit's freedom and human responsibility together without resolving them into a neat system. Faithful Christians in different traditions weigh this differently, and a group that respects the text will resist easing the discomfort by denying either side.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Do you believe you contributed something decisive to your own salvation, or have you ever stood still before the thought that you were dead and Someone made you alive?
sessions.practice: This week, write down the story of how you came to faith, or how you're still coming, in plain words. As you write, mark every place where you can see Someone working on you before you ever moved toward God: the conversation you didn't seek, the verse that wouldn't leave you, the grief that softened you. Don't credit yourself with the parts that were the wind. If you can't find your own story yet, write the name of the person whose coming to faith you most long for, and pray for the wind to blow there.
sessions.closingPrayer: God who hovered over the waters and raised your Son from the tomb, we were dead and you made us alive, and we did nothing to deserve it and nothing to accomplish it. Forgive us for taking the credit, for treating the new birth as our clever decision rather than your mercy. Thank you for every person in this room you've raised, and for every one of us you found when we weren't looking for you. Blow again, here, on the hardest hearts we know and on our own cold places. You are the Lord and giver of life. Give it. Amen.
reflection: When I tell the story of my faith, who is the main actor, and is that true?
Where in my coming to Christ can I now see the Spirit working on me before I ever turned toward God?
Whom have I quietly given up on as too far gone, and what does the new birth as resurrection say about that?
sessions.teaching:
Jesus has a conversation at night with a man named Nicodemus, and everything about the setting tells you to expect a gentle word. Nicodemus is a Pharisee, "a ruler of the Jews" (John 3:1), a teacher of Israel, a man who has kept the law and studied the Scriptures and done, by every visible measure, everything right. He comes respectfully: "Rabbi, we know that you are a teacher come from God" (John 3:2). And Jesus, instead of commending him, says the hardest thing he says to anyone about salvation: "Truly, truly, I say to you, unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God" (John 3:3).

Notice where that lands. The demand for a new birth is aimed not at the worst sinner in the city but at one of the best men in the room. That undoes a belief most of us carry, that respectability gives us a head start with God, that the moral person is closer to the kingdom than the immoral one. Jesus says no. The good man and the bad man need the same thing, and it isn't improvement. It's birth. If anything, the respectable man is in more danger, because his decency is a better disguise. The obvious sinner at least knows he's in trouble. The good man has spent his life building a case that he's fine, and the better the case, the harder it is to hear that it counts for nothing here.

Nicodemus is baffled in exactly the right way: "How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter a second time into his mother's womb and be born?" (John 3:4). He has stumbled onto the offense without understanding it, because birth is the one thing you can't do for yourself. You didn't plan your first birth or cooperate with it. You weren't consulted. You were brought into being by another. And Jesus says the second birth is like the first in this respect: "That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit" (John 3:6). The new birth isn't the old self improved, educated or persuaded. It's a dead thing made alive.

Now the objection, because it's a fair one and most of us feel it. Surely conversion is a decision. You hear the gospel, weigh it, and choose to believe. There's something real here. We do decide. The gospel calls for belief and repentance and means it, and no one is dragged kicking into the kingdom. Scripture holds human responsibility everywhere and never apologizes for it.

But Jesus puts in front of us what a decision can't explain. "The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit" (John 3:8). In Greek the same word, pneuma, means both wind and spirit, and Jesus is using both senses. You don't summon the wind or schedule it. You feel it when it comes and see what it does, but it blows on its own authority. The new birth is like that: truly your response, and truly his work.

I came to faith from atheism, and I can't take credit for it. That's true of every believer, wherever they started. A convinced skeptic can hear every argument for God and have an answer for each one, and the answers aren't stupid. Arguments matter, and I don't despise them. But you don't argue a dead man into breathing. Paul says we were "dead in our trespasses" until God "made us alive together with Christ" (Ephesians 2:5). What changes a person isn't finally a lost debate. It's the Spirit, a wind that starts to blow on someone who didn't ask for it and couldn't have produced it. And people who have been raised know, in a place arguments don't reach, that they didn't do it. God promised this long before Nicodemus: "I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you ... And I will put my Spirit within you" (Ezekiel 36:26-27).

Here's the most hopeful thing in this session. If the new birth is the Spirit's work and not the sinner's achievement, then no one you love is beyond it. Not the hardest skeptic or the most worn-out cynic or the one who has an answer for everything you could say, because the answer was never only an argument. The Spirit who hovered over the dark waters at the beginning and raised Jesus from the dead is in the business of making dead things alive. The dead don't climb toward life up a slope of persuasion. They're raised by a power outside themselves. So we don't give up on people because they seem too far gone. Too far gone is the only condition the Spirit has ever worked with. We were all there. So we pray for the wind, we speak the word the wind blows through, and we wait on the God who calls the dead by name.

scriptureStudy.note: "Unless one is born again he cannot see the kingdom of God." Not improved or reformed, but born. And the words are spoken to one of the most religious men in Israel.
"That which is born of the flesh is flesh ... The wind blows where it wishes." The new birth is the Spirit's work, felt and seen in its effects but never summoned or controlled by the one being born.

"I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you ... And I will put my Spirit within you." Centuries before Nicodemus, God promised the new heart as his own act, removing the heart of stone.
"Even when we were dead in our trespasses, made us alive together with Christ." The starting condition is death, and "made us alive" names the new birth as resurrection.

"He saved us, not because of works done by us in righteousness, but according to his own mercy, by the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit." Paul sets aside our righteous deeds as the cause and names the Spirit's renewing work.
"He has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead." The new birth is something God caused, rooted in his mercy and Christ's resurrection.
"Born, not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God." John rules out every human source of the new birth in a single line.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up an old conversation the church has never finished: the order of salvation. Does the Spirit make a person alive so that she can believe, or is believing the occasion of being made alive? The Reformed tradition, drawing on Augustine, argues that the dead can't believe until they're made alive, so regeneration comes first and faith is its fruit. Other traditions, Wesleyan and Arminian among them, stress the real and decisive response of the human will, enabled by grace that goes before it, and fear that putting regeneration strictly first turns the sinner into a passive object.

Don't try to score this debate quickly. Notice first what every side affirms: salvation is finally the Lord's, no one boasts before God, and the new birth is grace, not wages. Faithful churches differ on the order and remain one church. The task is to hold the mystery as Scripture does, refusing both a God who waits as a spectator for human permission and a human being with no real response. Weigh the pastoral stakes too, because how you answer shapes how you evangelize and how you pray. And come away sure of the thing all sides confess: "he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion" (Philippians 1:6), because he began it.

memoryVerse.text: That which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit. Do not marvel that I said to you, you must be born again.

sessions.title: The Fruit and the Walk
sessions.aim: To take the fruit of the Spirit as the slow growth of a real change worked from the inside, not a list of behaviors to manufacture, and to draw the line between fruit the Spirit grows and performance we produce to be seen.
sessions.summary:
Paul lists nine things and calls them "the fruit of the Spirit" (Galatians 5:22). Notice the words. Fruit, singular, and of the Spirit, not the works of the believer. The question for this session is the difference between fruit and performance, because the two can look the same from outside, and churches are full of people worn out from manufacturing what was meant to grow.

There are two errors, and each holds something true. One says growing in holiness is all effort: grit your teeth and try harder. It's right that Scripture commands us to put sin to death and walk by the Spirit. The other says it's all passive: let go and let God. It's right that we can't produce fruit by straining.

Jesus's picture of the vine and the branches holds both. A branch doesn't manufacture fruit, and it doesn't drift either. It stays joined to the vine, and fruit comes, slowly and unevenly, more like a season than a switch. Many believers still carry sins they assumed grace would have removed by now. The change is slow. The fruit grows at the speed of a tree, and we wanted it at the speed of a purchase.

keyScripture.why: "But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control ... If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (Galatians 5:22-23, 25). The change is the Spirit's fruit, and our part is a daily keeping in step, not a manufacturing of results.

discussion.q: Paul calls it the fruit of the Spirit, not the works of the believer. What changes when you hear your growth in love or patience as something grown in you rather than something you achieve?
discussion.behind: We instinctively hear the list as a to-do list and grind ourselves against it. Move the source from our effort to the Spirit's work, so the room can start telling the difference between bearing fruit and manufacturing it.

discussion.q: Fruit and performance can look the same from outside. Where have you produced the look of a virtue, kindness or patience, while inside it was effort to be seen?
discussion.behind: Press gently toward self-examination, not shame. We all perform virtues we don't have. Polished behavior can be empty. The Spirit grows the real thing slowly, while performance produces the fake thing fast.

discussion.q: Which are you more tempted by: holiness as gritted effort, or holiness as "let go and let God"? What's true in the one you resist?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. Strivers need to hear about abiding; drifters need to hear about walking and putting sin to death. Help each person find their own lean and receive the true thing in the error they're tempted to dismiss.

discussion.q: Many believers carry sins they assumed grace would have removed by now. Where has the slowness of your own change tempted you to give up or to fake it?
discussion.behind: This is the tender center. Slow change disillusions people and pushes them toward performance or despair. Help the room see that slowness is normal, that fruit grows at the speed of a tree, and that the answer is to keep walking. Go first, and be specific.

discussion.q: Read John 15:4-5 and Galatians 5:24-25. Jesus says "abide," and Paul says "keep in step." How do you hold those together without sliding into pure passivity or pure effort?
discussion.behind: The branch picture holds both: you stay connected and you keep walking, neither straining to produce nor idling in neutral. Help people name one concrete way they'll both abide and walk this week.

objections.objection: This fruit language is a softer way of saying "try harder." In the end I still have to produce love and patience and self-control, so calling it fruit is a comforting word for the same exhausting demand.
objections.response: Part of this is true. Scripture does command effort. Paul says, "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you" (Colossians 3:5), and "walk by the Spirit" (Galatians 5:16), and anyone waiting passively for holiness will wait forever. But notice what the word "fruit" changes. A branch does work, in a sense: it stays on the vine and doesn't break itself off. It doesn't strain to produce the apple. The apple is what comes from being joined to the vine's life. Your effort isn't the effort of manufacturing virtue by willpower. It's the effort of staying connected and keeping in step, putting yourself in the way of the Spirit's work through prayer, Scripture and obedience. That's why two people can do the same good deed and one bears fruit while the other only performs.

objections.objection: If the fruit is the Spirit's work and grows slowly on its own, I can stop trying and wait for it. Let go and let God. My job is to relax.
objections.response: Paul closes that door in the same passage. Right after the list he writes, "those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (Galatians 5:24-25). "Keep in step" is a walking word: an active, daily matching of your pace to another's. The let-go instinct is right that you can't manufacture fruit by gritting your teeth, but wrong that you therefore do nothing, because abiding isn't idleness. The branch that abides is doing the most active thing it can do, refusing to detach. You put sin to death, you walk, and you trust the fruit to the Spirit. As Paul puts it elsewhere, "if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live" (Romans 8:13).

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What virtue have you been performing for others while knowing, in the quiet, that the inside doesn't match the outside? What would it mean to stop performing it and ask the Spirit to grow the real thing?
sessions.practice: This week, pick the one piece of the fruit you most lack, maybe patience, self-control or kindness. Don't try to manufacture it by willpower. Each day, name it to the Spirit plainly: "I don't have this. Please grow it in me." Then put yourself in the way of the work: in prayer, in Scripture, and in the next ordinary chance to practice it. At the end of the week, write down not how much you produced but where you saw the smallest green shoot you didn't force.
sessions.closingPrayer: Spirit of God, we've tried to manufacture what only you can grow, and we're tired from the performance and ashamed of how little of the real thing there is in us after all these years. Forgive our impatience, and forgive the fake fruit we've hung on bare branches to be admired. Keep us joined to the Vine. Teach us to walk in step with you, neither straining as though everything depended on us nor drifting as though we had nothing to do. Grow your fruit in us at whatever slow pace is true, and give us the patience to keep walking while it comes. Amen.
reflection: Which am I more tempted by, the exhaustion of trying to manufacture holiness or the drift of waiting passively for it, and what's true in the error I resist?
Where has the slowness of my own change tempted me to give up, to fake it, or to decide the gospel doesn't work?
What does it mean, concretely, this week, for me both to abide in the Vine and to keep in step with the Spirit?
sessions.teaching:
Paul gives us a list we've heard so often it has worn smooth: "love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control" (Galatians 5:22-23). We tend to read it as a checklist of behaviors to muster. But look at what he calls it before he names a single item: "the fruit of the Spirit." Not the works of the believer, not the achievements of a disciplined Christian. Fruit, not product. Of the Spirit, not of you. And the word is singular, one fruit with nine flavors, grown by one source.

That matters because fruit and performance look the same from outside, and a lot of us are worn down from manufacturing what was meant to grow. So the question tonight is the difference between the two. If you can't tell them apart in your own life, you'll spend your years tired and faking it and wondering why holiness feels like a treadmill.

There are two errors, and most of us live in one of them. The first says growth in holiness is plain hard effort. Grit your teeth, try harder, and if you aren't growing it's because you aren't trying enough. There's something true in it. Scripture really does command effort. "Put to death therefore what is earthly in you," Paul writes (Colossians 3:5), and "walk by the Spirit" (Galatians 5:16). Someone waiting for holiness to settle on him like weather will wait until he dies. The second error says it's all passive. Let go and let God, stop trying, relax and let the Spirit do everything. There's truth in that one too. You can't manufacture fruit by straining. No amount of willpower has ever squeezed real patience out of an impatient heart. Each error holds something true, and each, on its own, does harm.

Jesus resolved this before Paul wrote the list. "I am the vine; you are the branches," he said. "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me ... apart from me you can do nothing" (John 15:4-5). The fruit isn't manufactured, because a branch doesn't perform fruit; it bears fruit from being joined to the vine's life. And the fruit isn't automatic, because the branch has one active, constant task: to stay joined, to refuse to detach.

Paul says the same at the end of his list: "If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit" (Galatians 5:25). Notice the order. "If we live by the Spirit" comes first. The life is already given; you didn't generate it. Then, "let us also keep in step." Walking doesn't produce the life. The life produces the walking. Someone who tries to keep in step without the life is only performing, and someone who has the life and won't keep in step is only drifting. Paul allows neither. So you stay joined to the Vine through prayer and Scripture and the company of other believers, and you keep in step through obedience and the daily putting to death of sin, and out of that joined, walking life the fruit grows: slowly, unevenly, in seasons, the way fruit has always grown.

I have to say something the church often avoids. Many believers are decades into this and still carry sins they assumed grace would have removed by now. I do. There are patterns brought to God a thousand times that are smaller than they were and not gone. When change is that slow, the temptation is to do one of two things: give up and decide the whole thing doesn't work, or start faking it, performing a patience we don't have and hanging plastic fruit on a branch so at least it looks alive. Both are refusals to walk.

Our impatient age can't stand this about fruit: it grows at the speed of a tree. You plant, you water, you wait through seasons when nothing seems to happen, and the growth is real but slow, and you can't pull a seedling taller with your hands. Paul says we "are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another" (2 Corinthians 3:18). Degree by degree. We wanted holiness at the speed of a purchase. God gives it at the speed of a harvest. And the patience to keep walking while the fruit comes is itself one of the nine. The Spirit grows the very thing slow growth requires.

So don't give up, and don't fake it. Stay on the Vine and keep in step. "He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:6). The Gardener hasn't abandoned a tree he planted.

scriptureStudy.note: "But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh." The command is a walk, active and ongoing, and the promise is that the way to resist the flesh is to walk with the Spirit.

"But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control." Fruit, singular, and of the Spirit: one cluster grown by one source, not nine separate achievements.

"And those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit." Putting sin to death and keeping in step belong together, which closes the door on passivity.
"Abide in me, and I in you ... apart from me you can do nothing." The branch bears fruit only by staying joined to the vine: you can't produce it yourself, and you must remain connected.
"He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion at the day of Jesus Christ." Slowness isn't abandonment. The God who started the change will finish it, on his timetable.
"We all ... are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit." The change is gradual, and it's the Spirit's work.
"If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live." By the Spirit, you put to death: neither pure effort nor pure passivity, but your action carried by his power.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at what the church has called the means of grace, because abiding and walking aren't vague moods. They've always had concrete shape. The tradition has named ordinary means through which the Spirit ordinarily works: reading and hearing Scripture, prayer, the Lord's Supper, and the gathered worship of the church. The Spirit is free, but he has promised to meet his people in these places, so neglecting them means stepping away from where the life flows.

Read J. I. Packer's Keep in Step with the Spirit (1984), which takes its title from Galatians 5:25. Packer argues for a growth in holiness that is neither the gritted self-effort of the moralist nor the "let go and let God" passivity of some holiness teaching, but an active dependence that holds effort and grace together. Set that beside our culture's expectation of quick results, and ask what that expectation does to believers whose change is real but slow. Weigh too the older language of mortification and vivification, putting sin to death and bringing righteousness to life, as two sides of one work of the Spirit. Waiting isn't wasted time. It's part of the work.

memoryVerse.text: If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.

sessions.title: Gifts and the Contested Question
sessions.aim: To set out the continuationist and cessationist cases at full and equal strength, to refuse to tell the group which is right, and to hold a room together in worship of the same Spirit across a divide that has separated faithful Christians for generations.
sessions.summary:
The Spirit gives gifts, and the church has argued hard about which ones still operate. Do tongues, prophecy and miraculous healing continue today, or did those gifts cease when the apostolic age closed and the New Testament was complete? This session doesn't settle it for the group. It sets out both positions at their strongest, because faithful, careful, Christ-loving believers hold each, and the divide runs through the middle of the godly.

The cessationist case, made by B. B. Warfield and Richard Gaffin among others, holds that certain gifts confirmed the apostles and the giving of Scripture, and that once the foundation was laid those gifts had done their work. It takes the sufficiency of Scripture with great seriousness and has grieved real abuses. The continuationist case, made by Gordon Fee and Sam Storms among others, holds that the New Testament never says the gifts will stop before Christ returns, and that Paul tells the church to "earnestly desire the spiritual gifts" (1 Corinthians 14:1). It takes the Spirit's present work with great seriousness and has grieved real deadness.

Then the turn. In the middle of the chapters most quoted in this argument, Paul writes about love. The gifts are real, and they aren't the point. What this session asks for isn't a position. It's a posture.

keyScripture.why: "Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit ... To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good" (1 Corinthians 12:4, 7). Every gift has one Giver and one purpose, building up the body, and that's the common ground beneath the argument about which gifts continue.

discussion.q: Before tonight, where did you land on whether gifts like tongues, prophecy and healing continue today? Where did that view come from: study, experience, or the church you grew up in?
discussion.behind: Bring the room's starting points into the open, along with where they came from. Many people hold a view they inherited rather than examined. You're not trying to change minds yet. You're noticing that background and experience shape our convictions here, which builds humility before the arguments come.

discussion.q: The cessationist argues that certain gifts confirmed the apostles and the giving of Scripture, served their purpose, and ceased. Put as its best defenders would put it, what's compelling about that case?
discussion.behind: Have the room build the cessationist case fairly, continuationists included. The aim is to be able to state the other side so well its holders would agree. Don't let it be caricatured as unbelief or fear of the Spirit.

discussion.q: The continuationist argues that the New Testament never says the gifts will cease before Christ returns, and tells us to desire them. Put as its best defenders would put it, what's compelling about that case?
discussion.behind: Now have the room build the continuationist case just as fairly, cessationists included. Hold the two strong cases side by side so people feel the weight of both and the ease of neither. Don't let it be caricatured as chasing experience.

discussion.q: This study won't tell you which side is right. Does that frustrate you? What might that frustration show about how tightly we want to hold a question Scripture leaves more open than we do?
discussion.behind: Stay with the discomfort of an unsettled question. We want an answer. Ask whether our certainty here serves the body of Christ or our need to be right. Handle strong feelings gently.

discussion.q: Read 1 Corinthians 13:1-3. If your group split over this question, what would it look like to be right about the gifts and wrong about love?
discussion.behind: This is where the session lands. Help the room feel that fracturing over this would be the deeper failure, and invite them to say out loud that they'll hold the Spirit tightly and the disputed question loosely. Go first, and name your own temptation to look down on the other side.

objections.objection: The sign gifts have plainly ceased. Tongues, prophecy and miraculous healing belonged to the apostles, confirming the foundation of the church and the giving of Scripture. Now that the foundation is laid and the canon is complete, we don't need them, and what passes for them today is psychological or counterfeit.
objections.response: Serious believers hold this for serious reasons, so give it its full weight. The cessationist case, made by B. B. Warfield and Richard Gaffin among others, rests on real biblical observations. Certain gifts did cluster around the apostles; Paul speaks of "the signs of a true apostle" (2 Corinthians 12:12), and Hebrews says God "bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit" to confirm the message (Hebrews 2:3-4). The church, Paul says, is "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets" (Ephesians 2:20), and a foundation is laid once. Underneath is a precious commitment to the sufficiency of Scripture, and grief over real manipulation done in the Spirit's name. A continuationist has to grant this weight before answering: the abuses are real, and nothing claimed today can stand beside Scripture as new revelation. The cessationist isn't someone afraid of the Spirit. He's often a careful reader of the Bible guarding something true.

objections.objection: The gifts plainly continue. The New Testament never says they'll stop before Christ returns. Paul commands the church to earnestly desire them, especially prophecy, and the Spirit who gave them hasn't changed. To say God switched them off is to read a theory into a silence and to quench the Spirit.
objections.response: Serious believers hold this for serious reasons too. The continuationist case, made by Gordon Fee and Sam Storms among others, rests on real biblical observations. Paul writes, "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:1), and gives detailed instructions for ordering tongues and prophecy in worship, which would be strange to leave in Scripture if they were about to expire. The passage most often cited for cessation says that "when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:10), and continuationists argue that the perfect is Christ's return, when we see "face to face" (13:12), not the completion of the New Testament, which the passage doesn't mention. A cessationist has to grant this weight before answering: there's no clear expiration date in the text, and Paul did say, "Do not quench the Spirit" (1 Thessalonians 5:19). The continuationist isn't a thrill-seeker. He's often a careful reader of the Bible refusing to silence a text.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: On a question where faithful Christians have long disagreed, is your certainty serving the unity of Christ's body, or your need to be right and to look down on those who differ?
sessions.practice: This week, do the harder of two things, depending on where you stand. If you're a settled cessationist, read one careful continuationist making the case at its best, and pray, "Spirit, show me what's true in this that I've dismissed." If you're a settled continuationist, read one careful cessationist making the case at its best, and pray the same prayer. Whichever you are, write down one thing the other side sees that you'd been quick to wave away, and one place where your certainty has carried contempt.
sessions.closingPrayer: Holy Spirit, you give your gifts as you will, for the common good, and we've turned your gifts into a battlefield and your body into camps. Forgive us for the contempt we've carried toward brothers and sisters who love you, read the same Scriptures, and land somewhere else. Teach us to hold the disputed question with open hands, and to hold you, your church, and the love that outlasts every gift with everything we have. Where we're wrong, correct us gently. Where we're right, keep us from pride. And above all our arguing, make us a people known by love. Amen.
reflection: Where did my view of the gifts actually come from: careful study of Scripture, my own experience, or the church that raised me? Have I ever examined the other side fairly?
Can I state the position I disagree with so well that its holders would say, "Yes, that's what we believe"? If not, what does that show me?
Have I carried contempt toward believers who differ from me on this, and what would it cost me to hold the question loosely and the Spirit tightly?
sessions.teaching:
This is the session most likely to make a room tense, which is why it needs the most care. The Spirit gives gifts, and the church has spent a long time arguing about which of them still operate. The question is plain even if the answer isn't. Do the gifts the New Testament calls tongues, prophecy and healing continue in the church today, or did those particular gifts cease when the age of the apostles ended and the New Testament was complete?

I'm going to do something that may frustrate you: I'm not going to tell you which side is right. That isn't a dodge. It's a conviction. This divide doesn't run between people who honor Scripture and people who chase experience. It runs through the middle of the godly. Some of the most careful, Christ-loving, Bible-soaked believers land on opposite sides, and a study that pretended otherwise would be misrepresenting the body of Christ. So I'll set out both cases as their own defenders would, leave the tie unbroken, and then show you what Paul does in the middle of the very chapters we argue over.

Take the cessationist case first, at its strongest. Certain gifts in the New Testament served to confirm that a true message was coming from a true messenger. Paul speaks of "the signs of a true apostle" (2 Corinthians 12:12), and Hebrews says God "bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit" to the message of salvation (Hebrews 2:4). Those gifts gathered around the apostles, and the apostles had a unique, unrepeatable role. The church is "built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone" (Ephesians 2:20), and you lay a foundation once. So the cessationist concludes that once the foundation was laid and the Scriptures were complete, the gifts that confirmed the founders had done their work. Underneath is something precious: a firm commitment to the sufficiency of Scripture, a refusal to add new words from God to a finished Word, and grief over manipulation and spiritual abuse done in the Spirit's name. B. B. Warfield made this case forcefully in Counterfeit Miracles (1918), and Richard Gaffin has made it carefully in our own time. Neither is a man afraid of God.

Now the continuationist case, at the same strength. Nowhere does the New Testament say the gifts will stop before Christ returns. Scripture speaks often about the present age and the last days and never says the gifts belong only to its opening years. Paul writes, "Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy" (1 Corinthians 14:1), and gives practical instructions for ordering tongues and prophecy in worship, which would be odd to leave in the Bible if those gifts were about to expire. The text most often cited for cessation says that "when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away" (1 Corinthians 13:10). Continuationists argue that the perfect is Christ's return, when we will see "face to face" (13:12), not the closing of the canon, which the passage never mentions. So, they say, the burden of proof lies with the one who claims God stopped. Underneath is something precious here too: a refusal to "quench the Spirit" (1 Thessalonians 5:19), and grief over a cold Christianity that has retired the living God to a doctrine. Gordon Fee pressed this case in God's Empowering Presence (1994), and Sam Storms has made it carefully. Neither is a thrill-seeker.

There are the two cases. Faithful churches divide over this; the creeds don't settle it, and it isn't a test of whether someone is a Christian. I'm leaving it there, and I'd ask you to sit in that discomfort, because it's teaching you something about how tightly you want to hold a question that faithful Christians have disagreed about for a very long time.

Now the turn that matters more than any answer. Between the chapter that lists the gifts and the chapter that puts them in order, Paul stops and writes this: "If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing" (1 Corinthians 13:1-2). Notice where he put it. Not in a letter about marriage or friendship, but right in the middle of the argument about gifts, as if to take the Corinthians, and us, by the shoulders and say: you're about to make this the whole thing, and it isn't.

The gifts are real. They aren't the point. A church that gets cessation exactly right and treats the continuationists down the road with contempt is a noisy gong. A church that gets continuation exactly right and looks down on the cautious cessationist is a clanging cymbal. I've felt that contempt rise in me, in both directions at different times. So what I'm handing you isn't a position. It's a posture: hold the disputed question with open hands, and hold the Spirit, his church, and the love that outlasts every gift with everything you have. "Love never ends" (1 Corinthians 13:8). When the perfect comes, however you read that phrase, the tongues will cease and the prophecies will pass, and the knowledge we argued over will give way to seeing him face to face. What will still be standing in that light is love.

scriptureStudy.note: "Now there are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit ... To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good." Whatever one believes about which gifts continue, they're never for display or status but for building up the body.
"One and the same Spirit, who apportions to each one individually as he wills." The Spirit chooses the gifts, which rebukes both the pride of the gifted and the envy of everyone else.

"If I speak in the tongues of men and of angels, but have not love, I am a noisy gong or a clanging cymbal." Paul sets the love chapter in the middle of the gifts chapters, putting the whole dispute under the one thing that outlasts every gift.

"As for prophecies, they will pass away; as for tongues, they will cease ... when the perfect comes, the partial will pass away." The central contested text: many cessationists read "the perfect" as the completed New Testament or the church's maturity, and continuationists as Christ's return.

"Pursue love, and earnestly desire the spiritual gifts, especially that you may prophesy." Paul commands love and the desire for gifts in one breath, which the continuationist presses and the cessationist must reckon with.
"Built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the cornerstone." The cessationist leans on this once-laid foundation and the apostles' unrepeatable role.

"God also bore witness by signs and wonders and various miracles and by gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to his will." The signs confirm the message; cessationists read this as a purpose now fulfilled, continuationists as an ongoing witness.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at the history of the question, which is older and more textured than modern shouting suggests. The view that the most striking gifts had largely ceased after the apostles was held in various forms through much of church history, and B. B. Warfield gave it a famous statement in Counterfeit Miracles (1918). Then came the Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles in 1906, the Pentecostal movement that grew from it, and later the charismatic renewal that reached nearly every denomination. A generation of careful scholars, among them Gordon Fee and Sam Storms, argued the continuationist case from the text, while Richard Gaffin's Perspectives on Pentecost (1979) restated the cessationist case from the apostolic foundation.

Read at least one strong voice from each side, ideally the side you instinctively oppose. Weigh the middle positions too, often called "open but cautious," held by those who don't rule the gifts out but test every claim and insist that nothing can stand beside Scripture. Weigh the pastoral danger on each side fairly: the deadness that can settle on a church that no longer expects God to act, and the chaos and manipulation that can overtake a church with no order and no testing. The aim isn't a manufactured agreement. It's a room that can disagree about a real and difficult question while remaining one body, under one Lord, filled with one Spirit.

memoryVerse.text: To each is given the manifestation of the Spirit for the common good.

sessions.title: The Spirit and the Groaning
sessions.aim: To meet the Spirit in our weakness, where we don't know how to pray and he intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words, and to receive his presence as the down payment of a new creation God has guaranteed.
sessions.summary:
Paul says something easy to read past: "we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26). What kind of God not only hears our prayers from above but prays within us when we've run out of words?

Romans 8 describes groaning in three layers. Creation groans, "subjected to futility" and waiting to be set free. We groan, as we wait for "the redemption of our bodies." And the Spirit groans within us, praying when we can't. Some will say this is just a religious name for wordless emotion. The caution is fair; not every feeling is God's voice. But Paul says more: the place where our prayer runs out is where the Spirit takes it up.

Then the last word of the study. The Spirit is called the "guarantee" of our inheritance, a down payment that binds God to finish what he started. The groaning isn't despair. Paul calls it "the pains of childbirth." The study doesn't end in ease. It leaves you groaning, with the Spirit groaning in you, toward a morning that's certain because God has put down the deposit himself.

keyScripture.why: "Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26). The Spirit prays within us precisely when we can't pray for ourselves.

discussion.q: Paul says "we do not know what to pray for as we ought." When have you sat down to pray and found you had no words? What did you assume that meant about you?
discussion.behind: Start with something almost everyone has known. Most people assume their wordlessness is a failure. Bring that assumption out so the passage can overturn it: the empty place isn't the end of prayer but where the Spirit takes it up.

discussion.q: What changes when you hear that your wordless ache isn't the failure of prayer but the place where God prays through you?
discussion.behind: This is the hinge. We treat the groan as prayer breaking down. Paul treats it as the place the Spirit's prayer begins. That's a great comfort to anyone worn out, so give it time.

discussion.q: Some would say calling our wordless ache the Spirit's intercession is just wishful labeling. What's true in that caution, and how is Paul saying more?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The caution against treating every feeling as God is healthy. But Paul names the Spirit as the one actually interceding, not our emotion renamed. Help the room keep that reverence without explaining the mystery away.

discussion.q: Read Romans 8:18-25. Paul says creation groans "in the pains of childbirth." How does calling your own groaning labor rather than dying change how you carry it?
discussion.behind: Labor pain is real agony, but it points toward life. Let the room feel that their groaning, and creation's, is the ache of something being born. That reframes suffering without making it smaller. Be gentle with anyone in a hard season.

discussion.q: The Spirit is called the "guarantee of our inheritance" (Ephesians 1:14). As we close the study, what does it mean to you that God has put a deposit of himself in you?
discussion.behind: Gather the five sessions: the Spirit we forgot, who gives new birth, grows fruit and gives gifts, and land on him as God's own pledge. Invite people to say what that deposit assures them of. Go first.

objections.objection: Calling my wordless ache the intercession of the Holy Spirit is wishful labeling. Sometimes I can't pray because I'm exhausted or empty or grieving, and dressing that up as God praying inside me is a story I tell to feel less alone.
objections.response: The caution is healthy. Not every feeling is God's voice, treating every emotion as the Spirit has done real harm, and a wordless ache can be only exhaustion or grief. Keep that honesty. But Paul says more than you're allowing him to. He doesn't say your groaning feels meaningful. He says "the Spirit himself intercedes for us," and that "he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God" (Romans 8:26-27). That isn't you relabeling your sadness. It's the claim that the God who lives in you prays through your weakness when you can't pray at all, so the emptiness you feared was the end of prayer is where some of the truest praying happens, by Someone who knows God's will perfectly.

objections.objection: If the Spirit is a down payment that guarantees the inheritance, why is there still so much groaning, mine and the world's? A guarantee that leaves everything broken doesn't feel like much of a guarantee.
objections.response: This is the ache of everyone still waiting, and Paul doesn't pretend the waiting is light. He says creation "was subjected to futility," that it groans "in the pains of childbirth," and that "we ourselves ... groan inwardly as we wait" (Romans 8:20-23). The guarantee doesn't remove the groaning, and that isn't a contradiction. A down payment is by definition not the full payment. It's the binding pledge that the rest is coming. So the Spirit in you isn't the absence of brokenness. He's God's deposit inside it, his costly promise that he'll finish. And Paul names the groaning as labor, not dying: a creation straining toward a life that's surely coming.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you've had no words to pray, did you carry it as your failure and your distance from God, when all along the Spirit may have been praying in you deeper than words could reach?
sessions.practice: This week, on a day you can't find words to pray, don't force them and don't give up. Sit quietly and say only, "Spirit, pray in me what I can't say." Then stop talking and let the silence and the ache be the prayer. Don't fill the quiet. Trust that the One who searches hearts knows the mind of the Spirit. Write down what it was like to let your weakness be the place of prayer rather than its end.
sessions.closingPrayer: Spirit of God, you meet us not at our strongest but at the bottom, where the words run out and the groaning begins, and you take up the praying we can't do. We've carried our wordlessness as shame and our weakness as distance from God, when all along you were interceding in us with groanings too deep for words. Thank you that the ache itself is being carried to the Father by you, who know his will perfectly. You are the down payment on a world being made new, God's own deposit in us, his pledge that morning is coming. Hold us in the labor until the birth. Amen.
reflection: Where have I treated my inability to pray as a failure, when Paul names it as the place the Spirit takes up the praying?
What in my life, or in the world, am I groaning over, and what changes if I call it labor toward a new creation rather than the slow dying of a broken one?
If the Spirit in me is God's down payment on an inheritance he has guaranteed, what does that assure me of on the days nothing feels certain?
sessions.teaching:
We end the study where the Christian life is actually lived, not at the height of our strength but at the bottom of our weakness, because that's where Paul puts the Spirit in Romans 8. "Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26). Notice that Paul includes himself in that "we." Not only new believers, but the apostle and the whole church, admitting there are times we sit down to pray and have nothing to ask, no words, only an ache.

That's where the good news is hidden. The Spirit we've studied for five weeks, fully God, the one who gives new birth, grows slow fruit and gives the gifts we argue about, doesn't stand back and wait for us to compose ourselves. He intercedes. He takes up the praying we can't do, within us. What kind of God is this? Not only one who hears prayer from his throne, but one who has come to live inside us and prays from there when we've run out of language.

Romans 8 describes the groaning in three layers, and you need all three to feel its weight. First, creation groans. Creation "was subjected to futility," Paul says, and "the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now" (Romans 8:20, 22). The whole world aches under its brokenness, waiting to be set free. Second, we groan: "we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (Romans 8:23). So groaning isn't a sign you lack the Spirit. It's a sign you have him, and so you feel the gap between what is and what's coming. Third, within our groaning, the Spirit groans, praying for us when we can't find the words. Creation's groan, ours, and God's own Spirit's, all in one labor.

Here's a fair objection. Someone says, "Calling my wordless ache the Spirit's prayer is wishful labeling. Sometimes I can't pray because I'm exhausted or grieving, and calling that God praying in me is a comforting story." The caution is healthy. Not every feeling is God's voice, the church has done real harm by treating every emotion as the Spirit, and a wordless ache can be only tiredness. Keep that honesty. But Paul says more than that. He doesn't say your groaning feels meaningful. He says the Spirit himself intercedes, and that "he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God" (Romans 8:27). This isn't you renaming your sadness. It's the claim that God, living in you, prays through your weakness when you can't pray at all. The empty place you feared was the end of prayer turns out to be where some of the truest praying in your life is happening, beneath your words, by Someone who knows exactly what to ask.

Then comes the word that ends the study. Paul gives the Spirit a particular name. In Ephesians he calls the Spirit "the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it" (Ephesians 1:14), and in 2 Corinthians he says God "has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee" (2 Corinthians 1:22). In Romans he calls him "the firstfruits." These are words from commerce and harvest, chosen on purpose. A guarantee in this sense is a down payment, a first installment that binds the giver to pay the rest. Firstfruits are the first sheaf of a harvest that's surely coming. So the Spirit in you is God's own deposit, his binding pledge to finish what he started.

That means the groaning isn't despair. Paul doesn't call it a death rattle. He calls it the pains of childbirth, and labor is agony that points toward life. Creation isn't running down toward nothing. It's straining toward a new creation God has guaranteed, and the Spirit in you is the proof.

So this study doesn't end tied up neatly, and it shouldn't, because we aren't home yet, and a study that put a bow on the Spirit would be untrue to the age we live in. It ends in groaning, but the groaning of labor, not of dying. And you don't groan alone. The God we admitted we'd forgotten, the one we treated as a force and left as a footnote, never forgot us. He's been here the whole time, in the room and in us, giving life, growing fruit, giving gifts, and now praying in us when we can't pray. We were the ones who went absent. He never did. Carry the groaning out of this room, but carry it knowing whose groan joins yours, and who has guaranteed how it ends.

scriptureStudy.note: "Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought." Paul puts the Spirit's help exactly at the point of our inability, so weakness in prayer isn't disqualification but the place the Spirit goes to work.

"He who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God." The Spirit's wordless prayer isn't vague feeling but prayer in line with God's will.

"The whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now. And not only the creation, but we ourselves ... groan inwardly." The groaning is named as labor, pain that points toward birth.

Paul says we have received "the Spirit of adoption," and that "the Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God." The Spirit who groans in our weakness also assures us of our place in the family.

"You ... were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the guarantee of our inheritance until we acquire possession of it." The Spirit is God's deposit, the binding pledge that the full inheritance is coming.
"Who has also put his seal on us and given us his Spirit in our hearts as a guarantee." The Spirit is the first installment God has placed in the believer, a pledge of what is promised in full.

"And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose." Coming right after the groaning and the Spirit's prayer, this promise doesn't deny the groaning. It's the assurance under which the labor is carried.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, follow the Spirit as firstfruits and guarantee across the whole story of redemption, because Paul's language in Romans 8 and Ephesians 1 carries a picture of the future the modern church has often lost. The New Testament doesn't picture Christian hope as souls escaping to a bodiless heaven but as "the redemption of our bodies" and the renewal of all creation, a new heavens and a new earth. N. T. Wright's Surprised by Hope (2008) argues this at length for a church that had quietly reduced its hope to going to heaven when we die.

Read the groaning of Romans 8 against that larger hope. Creation in labor isn't waiting to be thrown away but to be "set free from its bondage to corruption" (Romans 8:21), and the believer's aching body isn't a prison to escape but something to be raised. The Spirit links this age to the age to come: the firstfruits are the first sheaf of a harvest, and the down payment is the first installment of what is promised. So the Spirit in us now is a real foretaste of the life of the world to come, not only a promise about it. Set that against the despair that watches the world groan and concludes it's simply running down, and against the optimism that expects human progress to end the groaning. Then let it shape how you pray through weakness and how you endure.
