leaderPrimer:
Most of your group can describe two persons of the Trinity and will go quiet on the third. That's why this study exists. But vagueness isn't the leader's real hazard. Old wounds are. Someone at your table may have been told a healing failed because their faith was too small. Someone may have watched a church chase manifestations until Scripture got lost. Someone else may have been taught that expecting the Spirit to do anything today is error. Each of them will walk into session four, on the gifts, carrying that history.

That session is the live wire of the five, so know your own position and your own scars before you get there. A leader surprised by his own reactions can't steady anyone else's. The study handles the contested question by giving each side its strongest case and naming it as a question faithful churches divide on, not a test of faith. Your job is to keep that generosity in the room even if your own church has settled the matter. Especially then. But don't let the controversy swallow the study. It's one session; the Spirit is all five.

The quieter hazard is a group that talks about the Spirit for five weeks the way it would talk about glaciers, accurately and from a great distance. The Spirit isn't a force or an influence but a person, the one Jesus promised when he said, "I will not leave you as orphans" (John 14:18). Keep the study that personal. Let session two sit heavy, because being born of the Spirit offends every self-made instinct in the room. Let session five land gently on the Spirit who "intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26), because someone present may be in a season where that's the only prayer they have.

Invite expectancy without staging it. You can't schedule the wind, and the worst outcome of five weeks would be a room that learned to perform the Spirit's presence for one another. The best outcome needs no performance at all: a group that leaves less wary of the third person of the Trinity, and quietly hungrier for him.

faq.q: Is this study going to push my group toward speaking in tongues, or away from it?
faq.a: Neither, and it works hard to do neither. Session four takes up whether gifts like tongues, prophecy and healing continue today, and it sets out the continuationist and cessationist cases at full and equal strength, because faithful, careful, Christ-loving believers hold both. The divide runs through the middle of the godly, not between the faithful and the faithless. The study doesn't break the tie. Its concern is to hold a room together across the question, so a group can disagree about which gifts continue while worshiping the same Spirit. If you hoped it would arm you for the argument, you'll find instead a study that asks whether your certainty is serving the body of Christ or your need to be right.

faq.q: If I can't describe the Holy Spirit very well, am I a bad Christian?
faq.a: No, and the first session begins by admitting that this is most of us. Ask a room of lifelong believers to describe the Father and the Son and they'll manage it; ask who the Spirit is and watch the pause. Francis Chan called his book on this Forgotten God for a reason. The study treats this not as a private failure to scold but as a widespread loss to recover together. It argues that we forget the Spirit not because he's unimportant but because he's humble: he points to Christ, not himself. We mistook his self-effacement for absence. If the Spirit has been the vague one for you, you're exactly who this study is for.

faq.q: The study says conversion is the Spirit's work. Does that mean my decision to follow Christ didn't matter?
faq.a: No. Session two holds both truths at once. We really do decide, believe, repent and come. Scripture calls for all of that and means it, and the one who comes is truly responsible for coming. But the study won't let the human decision swallow God's act. Jesus doesn't tell Nicodemus to decide harder. He tells him he must be "born of the Spirit," and a birth is the one thing you can't perform on yourself. The church has long held that the same event is fully the Spirit's work and truly your response, the wind that blows where it wishes and the sail that really catches it. Christians in different traditions explain how those fit together differently, and the study leaves that second-order question open.

faq.q: Why does the study say no one can simply be argued into new life?
faq.a: Because that's what session two finds in John 3. Arguments matter; the study doesn't despise them, and the skeptic deserves good ones. But Jesus describes the new birth as the Spirit's work, like a wind no one commands, and Paul says we were "dead in our trespasses" until God "made us alive together with Christ" (Ephesians 2:5). That guards us from a mistake we're all prone to, thinking the unconverted only need the right case made. It also gives hope for the hardest skeptic you love, because the Spirit has never needed a person to be close already. Too far gone is the only condition he has ever worked with.

faq.q: Why won't the study just tell me whether the miraculous gifts have ceased?
faq.a: Because the divide on that question runs through the middle of the godly, and a study that handed you an answer would misrepresent the body of Christ. The cessationist case, made by theologians like B. B. Warfield and Richard Gaffin, takes the sufficiency of Scripture and the unique role of the apostles very seriously. The continuationist case, made by theologians like Gordon Fee and Sam Storms, takes the absence of any biblical expiration date and Paul's command to desire the gifts just as seriously. The study sets out both at full strength and then asks a harder question: can you hold the disputed point with open hands and the Spirit with everything you have? Paul put the great chapter on love in the middle of his chapters on gifts, as if to say a church right about gifts and wrong about love is a noisy gong.

faq.q: I've been a Christian for years and I'm not much more loving or patient than I was. Is something wrong with me?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Session three is built to say what the church often avoids: growth in holiness is slow. Paul calls love, patience and the rest "the fruit of the Spirit," and fruit grows at the speed of a tree, through seasons that can look like nothing is happening. Many believers carry sins they assumed grace would have removed by now. The slowness tempts us either to give up and decide the gospel doesn't work, or to fake it and hang plastic fruit on a branch. The study refuses both. Slowness isn't proof of failure. It's the ordinary pace of real change, and the patience to keep walking while the fruit comes is itself one of the nine.

faq.q: Isn't the fruit of the Spirit just a nicer way of telling me to try harder?
faq.a: No, though session three says plainly that effort is real and Scripture commands it. Paul says to put sin to death and to walk by the Spirit, and no one drifts into holiness. The word "fruit" marks the difference between manufacturing a virtue by willpower and bearing it from a connected life. Jesus gave the picture before Paul gave the list: the vine and the branches. A branch does the most active thing it can do, refusing to detach, and from that connection the fruit grows. So your effort isn't gritting your teeth to produce love. It's the effort of abiding and keeping in step with the Spirit through prayer, Scripture and obedience, while the fruit grows from the life you're joined to.

faq.q: What does it mean that the Spirit prays for me when I can't pray?
faq.a: Session five takes this from Romans 8:26: "we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words." Your wordlessness in prayer, the times you sit down with nothing to say, isn't the failure of prayer but the place where the Spirit takes it up. The Father "who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit," and the Spirit prays "according to the will of God" (Romans 8:27). The study is careful to say that not every feeling is God's voice. But Paul says more than that our groaning feels meaningful. He says God himself intercedes in us.

faq.q: The study keeps talking about groaning. Is it just telling me to expect suffering?
faq.a: It tells the truth about the age we live in, but it names the groaning carefully, and the name matters. Paul says the whole creation groans "in the pains of childbirth," that we groan inwardly, and that the Spirit groans within us. Childbirth is real agony, but it points toward life. So the groaning isn't the world running down toward nothing. It's creation straining toward a new creation God has promised. And the Spirit in you is called "the guarantee of our inheritance" (Ephesians 1:14), God's own deposit and pledge that he'll finish what he started. The study doesn't promise the groaning ends now. It promises that the One who began the labor has put down a deposit of himself.

faq.q: Does the study expect me to have some dramatic experience of the Spirit?
faq.a: No, and it refuses to engineer one. The leader's notes warn against staging an emotional experience so people feel they've met the Spirit, because the Spirit is God and not a feeling we summon. The study presents him as a person to be known, grieved, welcomed and walked with over a lifetime, not a sensation to chase on a given night. It honors the truth that the Spirit fills and moves, while refusing to reduce him to feelings or to call every impulse divine guidance. What it asks of you isn't an experience but a relationship, tested by Scripture, with the God who already lives in you whether or not the room feels charged.

faq.q: Why does the teaching keep including the writer and the leader instead of just teaching about the Spirit?
faq.a: Because no one teaches this from above it. I don't stand outside the forgetting this study names, the Trinity confessed on Sunday and the indwelling God ignored all week. I'm still learning to know the Spirit. The study asks every leader to bring the same candor, because you can't lead people toward a God you've functionally forgotten, and a leader who claims to have the Spirit figured out will ring hollow even when the doctrine is sound. A leader who can say, "I'm only beginning to know this person of God myself," can lead the room without pretense, and pretense is the one thing that would sink a study about the living presence of God.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't this just Christians describing their feelings and calling it God?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and the study tries to earn an answer. It doesn't ask you to relabel your emotions as divine; it warns Christians against doing exactly that. It grounds the Spirit's personhood in specific claims you can examine: Scripture says he can be lied to, grieved and resisted, things you can only do to someone. And it describes a new birth that no argument produces, the work of a presence an unbeliever has no category for. You can weigh that claim and find it unconvincing, and the study doesn't pretend it's a proof. But it isn't a believer dressing up a mood. It's a claim that there's a personal God who makes the dead alive, and you're invited to examine the claim, not to manufacture a feeling.

faq.q: How do I lead the session on spiritual gifts without my group falling into an argument?
faq.a: Carefully. The leader's notes treat this as the greatest danger in the study. The discipline is to state the position you disagree with so faithfully that its best defenders would recognize themselves in your words. If you're a settled cessationist, make the continuationist case so well that continuationists feel honored, and if you're a settled continuationist, do the same for the cessationist. Don't break the tie for the group. A leader who turns this into a vote will lose half the room and teach the other half contempt. When someone starts arguing to win rather than to understand, slow things down and turn the room back to listening, and back to the love Paul set in the middle of the gifts chapters.

timeline.event: "The Spirit of God was hovering over the face of the waters" (Genesis 1:2). The Spirit is present and active at creation, no latecomer to the story but the breath of God at work from the first page.

In exile, Ezekiel promises that God will give his people a new heart, remove the heart of stone, and put his Spirit within them (Ezekiel 36:26-27), regeneration promised as God's own act long before Jesus speaks to Nicodemus.
On the night before the cross, Jesus promises the disciples "another Helper," the Spirit of truth, to be with them forever and to dwell in them, a personal presence of the same kind as himself.
After the resurrection and ascension, the Spirit is poured out at Pentecost with a sound like a rushing wind and tongues as of fire, and the waiting church is sent into the world.
Paul writes to the Corinthians on spiritual gifts, naming their variety, their one Giver and their one purpose, and sets in the middle of the discussion his great chapter on love.
Paul writes to the Romans that the Spirit helps us in our weakness, interceding with groanings too deep for words, and that the whole creation groans in the pains of childbirth.

Some in the church grant that the Spirit is more than a creature but refuse to call him fully God. Athanasius answers them in his letters to Serapion, and the controversy forces the church to say plainly what it believes about the Spirit.
Basil of Caesarea writes On the Holy Spirit, arguing that the Spirit is to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Son, which makes sense only if the Spirit is fully God.

The Council of Constantinople expands the Nicene Creed to confess the Holy Spirit as "the Lord and giver of life," who proceeds from the Father and with the Father and the Son is worshiped and glorified.

Martin Luther writes Against the Heavenly Prophets, insisting against radical reformers that the Spirit works through the outward Word and sacraments, not apart from them, tying the Spirit's work to Scripture against both dead formalism and untethered enthusiasm.
The Azusa Street revival in Los Angeles helps launch the modern Pentecostal movement, reopening across the worldwide church the question of whether the miraculous gifts continue.

B. B. Warfield publishes Counterfeit Miracles, arguing that the miraculous gifts belonged to the apostles and their confirming work and ceased with the apostolic age, the most influential modern statement of cessationism.
Gordon Fee publishes God's Empowering Presence, a major study of the Spirit in Paul's letters and a serious exegetical case for the Spirit's continuing gifts.
Francis Chan publishes Forgotten God, calling the church to reckon with how thoroughly it has neglected the Holy Spirit.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thanks for being here, and for being willing to spend five weeks on the person of the Trinity most of us know least. Three things before we start. First, this is a safe room. You can say here that you've never really known the Holy Spirit, that he's been the vague one for you, and no one will make you feel foolish, because that's most of us. Second, this study won't push you toward speaking in tongues or away from it. When we reach the session on gifts, we'll set out both sides at their strongest and leave the question open, because faithful Christians who love the same Lord land on opposite sides of it. Third, I'm inside all of this with you. I know the doctrine and still live some days as though God were far off. We're not experts standing over the Spirit. We're people only beginning to know the God who has been living in us the whole time. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. Let me read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it before anyone says anything. There are no wrong answers in the first five minutes.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what the passage says about the Spirit. Now let's bring it home, into the ordinary week: the prayers we don't know how to pray, the change that comes slower than we want, and the God we keep forgetting is already in the room. That's where this either matters or doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We'll stop there, even though it doesn't tie up neatly. The Spirit is God, and he won't fit inside a tidy summary, and the best thing we can do is keep walking with him rather than pretend we've figured him out. This week, take this toward the Spirit himself rather than only thinking about him. Try the practice. Sit with the reflection questions on your own. And if tonight stirred a hunger to know this person of God, follow it. He has been waiting, with great patience, to be known. Let me pray for us before we go.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, set the ground rules about safety and about the gifts session to come, and walk slowly through session 1's opening questions. Begin practicing speaking of the Spirit as a person.
Week 2: Session 1, The Spirit We Ignore, full discussion and practice on the personhood and deity of the Spirit.
Week 3: Session 2, Born of the Spirit, with extra time on the new birth as resurrection.
Week 4: Session 3, The Fruit and the Walk, part one: the difference between fruit and performance, and the two errors about growth in holiness.
Week 5: Session 3 continued: the vine and the branches, abiding and walking, and time on the slowness of real change.
Week 6: Session 4, Gifts and the Contested Question, with extra time to build both the cessationist and continuationist cases at full strength.
Week 7: Session 5, The Spirit and the Groaning: the Spirit who intercedes in our weakness and the Spirit as the down payment of the new creation.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit the five practices and the Scripture index, share what each person now wants to bring to the Spirit, and leave room for anyone unsure about the new birth to talk.

Week 2: Session 3, The Fruit and the Walk, with extra time on abiding and the slowness of growth in holiness.
Week 3: Session 4, Gifts and the Contested Question, both cases built at full strength and the unity of the body guarded.
Week 4: Session 5, The Spirit and the Groaning, with a short closing on the Spirit as God's down payment in us.

glossary.definition: The third person of the one God, of one being with the Father and the Son, fully divine and fully personal, who can be grieved, lied to and resisted, and who has come to live in the people of God. Not a force or an influence but God himself, present and indwelling.

The new birth: the Spirit's act of making the spiritually dead alive, which Jesus calls being "born again" or "born of the Spirit." Not the improvement of the old self but a resurrection, something God does in us.

The Spirit's living presence in the believer, the "with you" and "in you" Jesus promised, so that a Christian isn't visited by God from a distance but inhabited by him. The believer's body is "a temple of the Holy Spirit" (1 Corinthians 6:19).

Love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness and self-control, which the Spirit grows in the believer. Called fruit rather than works because it comes from a connected life, not from willpower.

The slow, lifelong work by which the Spirit makes a believer actually holy, growing fruit at the speed of a tree. Lived as abiding in the Vine and keeping in step with the Spirit, between the errors of gritted self-effort and passive waiting.
The varied gifts the Spirit gives believers as he wills, for the common good and the building up of the church, never for status or display. Which of them continue today is a long-disputed question.

The view that certain miraculous gifts, such as tongues, prophecy and healing, served to confirm the apostles and the giving of Scripture and ceased once the apostolic foundation was laid. Held by serious believers for serious reasons, and set out at full strength in session 4.

The view that the New Testament names no end date for the gifts before Christ returns, that Paul tells believers to desire them, and that they continue in the church today. Held by serious believers for serious reasons, and set out at full strength in session 4.

The practice this study asks for on contested questions: putting the view you disagree with so faithfully that its best defenders would recognize themselves in your words, and refusing to caricature the other side in order to win.

The Spirit's praying within the believer, taking up the prayer we can't make and interceding "with groanings too deep for words" (Romans 8:26) at the point where our own words run out, according to the will of God.

The ache of creation, the believer, and the Spirit in Romans 8, which Paul calls "the pains of childbirth": agony that points toward birth, not death, as creation strains toward the redemption God has promised.

The Spirit named as the down payment, seal and firstfruits of the believer's inheritance (Ephesians 1:14; 2 Corinthians 1:22). A first installment that pledges the giver to pay in full: God's own deposit that he'll finish what he started.

The confession, set down at Constantinople in 381, that the Spirit "proceeds from the Father," eternally and not as a creature. The church used this language to guard the Spirit's full deity within the one God.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Most of us could describe the Father and the Son and then go quiet on the Holy Spirit, the forgotten person of the Trinity we treat as a power source and an afterthought. This five-session study recovers the Spirit as fully God and fully personal: who he is, the new birth he alone brings, the slow growth of his fruit, the contested question of the gifts (with both sides given their strongest case), and the Spirit who prays in us when we have no words. It won't settle the gifts debate for you, and it works to hold the room together across it. Any volunteer can lead it with no preparation.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on the Holy Spirit, the person of the Trinity most of us know least. Before anyone worries: it won't push you toward speaking in tongues, and it won't push you away. When we reach the session on gifts, we'll set out both sides at their strongest and leave the question open, because faithful Christians who love the same Lord disagree about it. The study presents the Spirit as a person we can know and walk with, not a force we switch on. I'm only beginning to know him myself. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: We can describe the Father and the Son and go quiet on the Holy Spirit. A five-session study on the forgotten person of the Trinity: the God who makes the dead alive and prays in us when we have no words. It sets out both sides of the gifts debate at full strength, leaves the question open, and presents the Spirit as a person to know rather than a power to use.
quoteCards: You can't grieve a force or lie to the wind. The Spirit is a person, and we've treated God himself as a vapor.
We don't forget the Spirit because he's unimportant. We forget him because he's humble. He points away from himself to Christ.
You didn't assist in your first birth, and you didn't author your second. The dead don't rise. They're raised.
You don't argue a dead man into breathing. The new birth is the Spirit's work.
We wanted holiness at the speed of a purchase. God gives it at the speed of a harvest.
A church right about the gifts and wrong about love is a noisy gong.
Your wordless ache isn't the failure of prayer. It's where the Spirit prays for you.
The groaning isn't the world running down. It's the labor pain of a creation being made new.
